activity.check: Name the denominator for each month. A lower count need not mean a lower rate.
activity.modelAnswer: Count change: (80 - 100)/100 x 100 = -20%, a 20% fall. March: 100/1,000 x 100 = 10%; April: 80/800 x 100 = 10%. Fewer appointments were missed, but the missed proportion stayed the same. These figures do not support improved reliability measured by that rate, or show that any individual changed.
activity.whyAdequate: It verifies the true count claim while rejecting the unsupported move from a lower count to improved attendance per booked visit.

exitTicket.title: More missing assignments?
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: A course recorded 18 missing assignments out of 120 assignments due in September, and 20 out of 200 due in October. The teacher says, 'More assignments were missing, so the missing-assignment rate got worse.'
exitTicket.output: Write both rates and two sentences assessing the teacher's conclusion.
steps: Calculate each month's missing rate: missing assignments / assignments due x 100.
State which month has the higher missing count and which has the higher missing rate.
Explain whether the claim about a worsening rate follows, without claiming that these figures identify a cause.
exitTicket.check: Use assignments due as the denominator; do not divide by a number of students that was never supplied.
exitTicket.modelAnswer: September: 18/120 x 100 = 15%. October: 20/200 x 100 = 10%. October has the higher missing count, but September has the higher missing rate. The claim about a worsening rate does not follow; the rate fell, and these figures alone do not explain why.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: It uses the supplied totals, distinguishes count from rate, and avoids adding an unsupported causal explanation.

discussion.prompt: Can the lower count still matter even when the rate stays the same?
discussion.guidance: Yes. A count can matter for workload or capacity, while a rate answers a different question about the proportion of opportunities missed. Name the question before choosing a measure.

discussion.prompt: What would we need to say that particular patients became more reliable?
discussion.guidance: We would need records comparing those individuals over time. Aggregate appointment totals do not identify who changed or why.

misconceptions.misconception: A smaller count always means a smaller rate.
misconceptions.response: The total can also shrink. Calculate count divided by its relevant total.

misconceptions.misconception: The denominator can be whichever total is easiest to find.
misconceptions.response: It must match the claim. For a missed-appointment rate, use booked appointments for the same period.

misconceptions.misconception: A falling rate shows what caused the improvement.
misconceptions.response: A rate describes a pattern. Explaining its cause needs additional evidence.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Give a three-column table headed count, relevant total, rate. For March, enter 100, 1,000, and 100/1,000 x 100 = 10%. Ask learners to complete the April row using 80 and 800.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask how to describe the exit-ticket rate change in percentage points. Define this as new percentage minus old percentage. Expected calculation: 10% - 15% = -5 percentage points, not a fall of 5% of the old rate.

assessmentCriteria: Each calculation uses the relevant total for the same period.
The percentage calculations are correct and clearly labelled.
The conclusion distinguishes count from rate and avoids unsupported personal or causal claims.

packs.title: Separate a change from its cause
packs.subtitle: Notice what changed, then ask what evidence would identify the cause.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Distinguish an observed change from a claim about its cause.
Identify a simultaneous change that could explain the result.
Propose a comparison that separates two possible causes.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the three scenarios and their model answers.
Print the three-page handout or display one activity at a time.
Explain that all scenarios and figures are invented for reasoning practice.

vocabulary.definition: Something that helps produce an outcome.
A group used to judge what might happen without the change being tested.
Using chance to decide which groups receive a change, helping avoid systematic differences.

timeline.title: Spot the competing changes
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the fruit-sales warm-up. Compare the observed outcome with the manager's explanation.

timeline.title: Separate lighting from patrols
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the street-lighting activity. Check that their proposed comparison changes lighting while keeping patrol conditions comparable.

timeline.title: Test the comparison
timeline.instructions: Discuss the supplied prompts and model answer. Ask whether another change is still tied only to the treatment group.

timeline.title: Transfer the method
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the attendance exit ticket independently. Assess the observation, alternative cause, and proposed comparison.

warmup.title: Why did fruit sales rise?
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: A cafeteria sells more fruit in the week it displays healthy-eating posters. That week it also cuts fruit prices. The manager says the posters caused the rise.
warmup.output: Write an observation, another possible cause, and one sentence explaining why the posters have not been isolated.
steps: State what happened without naming its cause.
Name the other change and explain how it could affect sales.
Explain why these facts cannot establish the effect of posters alone.
warmup.check: Have you kept an observed rise separate from an explanation for it?
warmup.modelAnswer: Observation: fruit sales rose. Lower prices could encourage purchases. Because posters and prices changed together, the rise does not show how much, if any, came from the posters.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer identifies a relevant competing change without claiming to know which cause mattered.

activity.title: Lighting, patrols, and theft reports
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: Reported thefts on a street fall from 50 in September to 35 in October. Brighter lights are installed at the start of October, and extra evening patrols begin that same day. The mayor says the lights caused the drop.
activity.output: Write the observation, a competing explanation, and a proposed comparison in three labelled parts.
steps: State the observed change separately from the mayor's causal explanation.
Name the other change that could explain some or all of the drop.

Propose a comparison that would help separate the effects: describe which streets to compare and which other condition should be kept similar. Do not claim your proposed comparison has already been done.
activity.check: Does the comparison vary lighting without also giving only the newly lit streets extra patrols?
activity.modelAnswer: The observation is that reports fell from 50 to 35 after two changes. Extra patrols are a rival explanation. Compare similar streets over the same period, some receiving brighter lights and others retaining existing lights, while keeping patrol levels comparable; random assignment of lighting would make the test stronger where feasible.
activity.whyAdequate: It identifies the simultaneous change and proposes evidence that could distinguish explanations instead of treating 'after' as 'because of'.

exitTicket.title: Why did absences fall?
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: Weekly absences in a school fall from 12 to 5 after text reminders and a new bus service begin on the same day. The principal credits the reminders alone.
exitTicket.output: Write the observed change, another possible cause, and a comparison that could test reminders.
steps: State the observed change without attributing a cause.
Name the other change and explain its possible effect.
Describe groups to compare and which other condition must stay comparable.
exitTicket.check: Would your comparison give similar bus access to students with and without reminders?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Absences fell from 12 to 5. The bus service might make attendance easier. Compare similar student groups over the same period, with comparable bus access, giving reminders to one group and not the other; random assignment where feasible would strengthen the comparison.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The answer separates the outcome from its explanation and proposes varying reminders without tying them to better bus access.

discussion.prompt: Does another possible cause prove the lights had no effect?
discussion.guidance: No. It prevents assigning the drop to lights alone. Lighting, patrols, both, or other factors might matter.

discussion.prompt: Why compare streets during the same period?
discussion.guidance: Shared timing helps reduce differences such as seasonal changes. It does not guarantee that the streets are otherwise comparable.

misconceptions.misconception: After a change means because of that change.
misconceptions.response: Timing can support a causal account, but simultaneous changes and missing comparisons must be considered.

misconceptions.misconception: Finding a rival explanation disproves the first one.
misconceptions.response: A plausible rival shows uncertainty; further evidence is needed to separate their contributions.

misconceptions.misconception: Any two groups make a fair test.
misconceptions.response: Groups should be comparable in relevant ways. Random assignment helps but does not excuse inconsistent measurement.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Use three headings: what changed, what else changed, what to compare. Let learners say their comparison aloud before writing it. Expected example: fruit sales rose; prices also fell; compare poster and no-poster settings with comparable prices.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask: If brighter-light streets also get more patrols in the proposed comparison, what remains unresolved? Expected response: the effects remain mixed, so a difference cannot be attributed to lighting alone.

assessmentCriteria: The observed outcome is stated separately from its proposed cause.
A supplied competing change is linked plausibly to the outcome.
The proposed comparison varies the target factor while keeping the competing condition comparable.

packs.title: Test another explanation
packs.subtitle: Generate plausible alternatives and ask what could distinguish them.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Explain how more than one account could fit an observation.
Use supplied details to propose plausible alternatives.
Name evidence that could help distinguish two explanations.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the three scenarios and their model answers.
Print the three-page handout or display one activity at a time.
Explain that all scenarios and figures are invented for reasoning practice.

vocabulary.definition: Another account that could fit the same observation.
A description of how a proposed cause could produce the outcome.

timeline.title: Offer a plausible alternative
timeline.instructions: Use the cafe warm-up. Require a link between the new office and possible customers, not just a label.

timeline.title: Explain three museum possibilities
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the museum activity, explaining how each supplied change could influence visits.

timeline.title: Choose evidence that separates accounts
timeline.instructions: Discuss model answers and prompts. Check that proposed comparisons vary the factor of interest rather than changing everything together.

timeline.title: Test transfer independently
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the library exit ticket. Assess whether their alternatives remain possibilities and their comparison is relevant.

warmup.title: The cafe gets busier
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: A cafe's lunchtime visits rise during the week it introduces music. A large office opens next door that same week. The owner credits the music.
warmup.output: Write one alternative explanation and one sentence stating what remains unknown.
steps: Use the new office to give an alternative to the music explanation.
Explain how it could increase lunchtime visits.
State whether the facts show which explanation contributed more.
warmup.check: Have you explained a connection while avoiding an unsupported verdict?
warmup.modelAnswer: The new office could bring nearby workers looking for lunch. The facts do not show how much the music or the office contributed, and both could matter.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer supplies a plausible mechanism and preserves uncertainty between compatible explanations.

activity.title: Why did museum visits rise?
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: A museum's family visits rise from 200 to 320 during the first weekend of free admission. That weekend also brings a new dinosaur exhibit, a school holiday, and unusually heavy rain. The museum credits free admission alone.
activity.output: Write three possible explanations with reasons, then one proposed comparison for a chosen rival.
steps: List three rival explanations using the supplied details.
For each, write one sentence explaining how it could increase museum visits. Mark these as possibilities, not established causes.
Choose one rival and name a comparison that would help distinguish it from the effect of price.
activity.check: Have you explained a plausible connection for each rival instead of merely listing coinciding events?
activity.modelAnswer: The dinosaur exhibit might attract interested families; the holiday might give them more free time; rain might make indoor activities more attractive. To examine the exhibit explanation, compare similar weekends with the same exhibit but different admission prices while keeping holiday and weather conditions as comparable as possible. The supplied facts do not tell us which cause contributed how much.
activity.whyAdequate: It supplies mechanisms for three alternatives and a relevant follow-up comparison without presenting possibilities as findings.

exitTicket.title: The library app launch
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: Library loans rise in the month a booking app launches. The library also extends opening hours and starts a popular reading challenge that month. The director credits the app alone.
exitTicket.output: Write two alternative explanations and one comparison that could help test the app.
steps: Explain how longer opening hours could increase loans.
Explain how the reading challenge could increase loans.
Describe a comparison with and without the app that keeps the other two changes comparable.
exitTicket.check: Are your explanations possibilities, and would the comparison separate the app from the other changes?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Longer hours could let more people borrow; the challenge could motivate more borrowing. Compare similar branches over the same period, some with the app and some without, with comparable hours and the same challenge. These facts alone do not assign the increase to any one change.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The answer links each rival to borrowing and proposes a comparison that could provide more informative evidence.

discussion.prompt: Must the rival explanations exclude one another?
discussion.guidance: No. Free admission, an exhibit, holidays, and weather could all influence visits. Their separate contributions remain unknown.

discussion.prompt: Does imagining a possibility make it equally likely?
discussion.guidance: No. A possibility needs a plausible connection and then evidence. Naming it does not establish its probability or importance.

misconceptions.misconception: Any story is a useful alternative.
misconceptions.response: A useful alternative fits the known facts and explains how the outcome could occur.

misconceptions.misconception: Listing a coincidence explains its effect.
misconceptions.response: State the mechanism: why might the event influence the outcome?

misconceptions.misconception: One plausible alternative settles the issue.
misconceptions.response: It opens a question. Seek evidence that distinguishes accounts, and allow multiple factors to contribute.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Provide the frame: [change] might lead to [action], which could increase [outcome]. Use the museum facts to complete one example together. Expected example: the new office could supply more nearby lunchtime customers; this remains a possibility.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask whether a rainy weekend with free admission compared with a dry paid weekend isolates price. Expected response: no; both price and weather differ, so either could help explain the difference.

assessmentCriteria: Alternatives use the supplied facts and fit the observed outcome.
Each alternative includes a plausible connection rather than a mere coincidence.
The proposed comparison could distinguish explanations without treating an untested possibility as a finding.

packs.title: Check the evidence you prefer
packs.subtitle: Notice selective attention and build a check that could change your mind.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Identify a stated pattern of selecting agreeable evidence.
Apply the same quality standards to supportive and critical evidence.
Propose a relevant outcome measure that can reveal a mistake.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the three scenarios and their model answers.
Print the three-page handout or display one activity at a time.
Explain that all scenarios and figures are invented for reasoning practice.

vocabulary.definition: A tendency to favor information that fits what we already believe or want to believe.
A rule for judging evidence quality, applied consistently to different conclusions.

timeline.title: Notice selective reading
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the headline warm-up. Focus on the stated behavior; do not infer hidden motives or whether the underlying claim is true.

timeline.title: Build a fair checking plan
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the study-app activity. Check that their plan includes critical reviews and a measure of learning.

timeline.title: Discuss what a bias does not prove
timeline.instructions: Use the discussion prompts and model answer to separate a flawed checking process from the truth of the claim.

timeline.title: Apply the checking method
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the planner exit ticket independently. Assess selection, consistent standards, and a relevant outcome measure.

warmup.title: Only the helpful headlines
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: Mina believes morning classes help learning. She saves three headlines agreeing with her and ignores two disagreeing headlines because she says, 'I only want support for my view.' She has not read any study methods.
warmup.output: Write the selection pattern and one fair next step.
steps: Identify which evidence Mina accepts and avoids.
Explain how that choice favors her existing view.
Propose a next step that uses the same evidence standards for both sides.
warmup.check: Have you identified the stated behavior without declaring her belief true or false?
warmup.modelAnswer: Mina selects agreement and avoids disagreement, favoring her prior view. She should inspect the methods and learning measures behind all five reports using the same criteria, rather than judging by headline agreement.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer diagnoses selective attention from explicit facts and proposes a check; it does not decide the claim from the bias alone.

activity.title: Does the study app help?
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: After buying a study app, Sam reads six glowing reviews and skips four detailed critical reviews because 'they will only make me doubt my choice'. Sam concludes the app must improve learning. No learning results have been collected.
activity.output: Write the selection pattern, a three-step checking plan, and a learning measure with an explanation.
steps: Identify the evidence Sam selects and the evidence Sam avoids, and explain the direction of the preference.
Write a three-step checking plan: include both kinds of reviews, use the same quality criteria for them, and collect a learning measure rather than relying only on praise.
Name a specific learning measure, such as a delayed quiz on comparable material, and say why review popularity alone is insufficient.
activity.check: Does your plan make it possible to discover that the purchase was unhelpful, or only reassure Sam?
activity.modelAnswer: Sam favours praise that confirms the purchase and avoids criticism that could challenge it. Plan: read all ten reviews; assess each for relevant experience and checkable evidence using the same criteria; compare delayed-quiz performance on comparable material studied with and without the app under similar conditions. Positive reviews show approval, not necessarily better learning.
activity.whyAdequate: It describes the selective attention and turns a vague request to 'be unbiased' into concrete checks capable of revealing a mistake.

exitTicket.title: Defending a new planner
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: After buying a planner app, Jo reads eight positive reviews and ignores three detailed complaints because 'I do not want to regret buying it'. Jo concludes the app reduces missed deadlines. No deadline records have been collected.
exitTicket.output: Write the biased selection and a three-step checking plan with a relevant measure.
steps: Identify the evidence Jo chooses and avoids, and the direction of the preference.
Plan to read both kinds of review and apply the same quality criteria.

Name a comparison using missed deadlines. You may compare rates: missed deadlines divided by total deadlines, using comparable workloads and periods. Explain why positive reviews alone do not answer the claim.
exitTicket.check: Could the plan reveal that the app does not reduce missed deadlines?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Jo favors approval and avoids criticism of the purchase. Plan: read all eleven reviews; judge each for relevant experience and checkable evidence; compare missed-deadline rates with and without the app for similar workloads. A rate is missed deadlines divided by total deadlines. Praise measures approval, not necessarily fewer missed deadlines.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The plan treats both sides consistently and measures the claimed outcome. A fair comparison would still need attention to workload and other differences.

discussion.prompt: Does finding bias show the app is ineffective?
discussion.guidance: No. It shows a problem with how the claim was checked. Better evidence may support or undermine the claim.

discussion.prompt: Must positive and negative reviews receive equal weight?
discussion.guidance: No. Apply equal standards, then weight the reviews according to their evidence quality. Equal numbers or equal conclusions are not required.

misconceptions.misconception: Calling someone biased settles the factual question.
misconceptions.response: Describe the behavior and inspect the evidence. A flawed process does not itself make a conclusion false.

misconceptions.misconception: Being fair means giving all reviews equal weight.
misconceptions.response: Use the same criteria; more relevant, checkable evidence can deserve more weight.

misconceptions.misconception: Bias requires a hidden bad motive.
misconceptions.response: These cases state the selective behavior directly. Do not claim access to thoughts or motives not supplied.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Use two columns, selected and avoided, before writing the plan. Offer review-quality questions: Is the experience relevant? Can the claim be checked? Expected example: read praise and criticism, check both for relevant experience and evidence, then compare a learning outcome.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask: If one negative review gives detailed learning results and six positive reviews only say "great", should their counts decide? Expected response: no; inspect methods and relevance, and do not assume either praise or criticism is reliable solely from its direction.

assessmentCriteria: The stated selective behavior and its direction are identified accurately.
The plan applies the same quality criteria to supportive and critical evidence.
The proposed outcome measure addresses the claim and can reveal an unhelpful result.

packs.title: Make the tradeoff visible
packs.subtitle: Compare gains, costs, and who bears them before recommending a choice.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: Identify a possible benefit, cost, and affected group.
Compare feasible allocations of a limited resource.
Explain how evidence and priorities can change a recommendation.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the three scenarios and their model answers.
Print the three-page handout or display one activity at a time.
Explain that all scenarios and figures are invented for reasoning practice.

vocabulary.definition: A gain in one respect accompanied by a cost or lost opportunity in another.
The benefit given up by using a limited resource for something else.

timeline.title: Name what is given up
timeline.instructions: Use the lunchtime warm-up to distinguish time gained for one activity from time lost for another.

timeline.title: Compare study-time allocations
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the school activity. Check that each allocation totals 60 minutes and that expected score gains remain unproven.

timeline.title: Discuss priorities and evidence
timeline.instructions: Compare the model answer and alternative feasible allocations. Ask learners to name who bears each cost.

timeline.title: Explain an independent choice
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the community-room exit ticket. Assess the budget, stated priority, tradeoff, and useful question rather than rewarding a particular preference.

warmup.title: A lunchtime choice
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: A class has a 40-minute lunch break. One proposal uses 10 minutes for quiet reading and leaves 30 minutes for eating and conversation. The current break allows all 40 minutes for eating and conversation.
warmup.output: Write one gain, one lost opportunity, and one group that could value that loss.
steps: Name the time gained for reading.
Name the time given up for another activity.
Identify students who could especially value the activity losing time.
warmup.check: Have you described both sides without assuming everyone has the same priority?
warmup.modelAnswer: The proposal adds 10 minutes of reading and removes 10 minutes available for eating or conversation. Students who need a longer eating break or value lunchtime social contact could especially value the lost time.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer identifies the fixed time budget and a possible affected group without deciding that one use is best for everyone.

activity.title: How should study time be used?
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: A school has 60 minutes each week for optional study activities. It proposes moving 30 minutes from open reading to test preparation. Teachers expect more exam practice, but no evidence yet shows a score gain. Students who rely on school reading time would lose half that time.
activity.output: Write a benefit, cost, and affected group; propose a feasible allocation; add one question to guide the decision.
steps: Make three labelled lines: possible benefit, cost, and affected group. Use the facts and distinguish an expected benefit from a demonstrated result.
Propose one alternative allocation of the 60 minutes and explain its tradeoff.
Write one question the school should answer before choosing a plan.
activity.check: Do all allocations total 60 minutes? Have you named who bears the cost rather than calling the proposal simply 'good' or 'bad'?
activity.modelAnswer: Possible benefit: more exam practice, with score improvement still unproven. Cost: 30 fewer minutes of open reading. Affected group: especially students dependent on school reading time. An alternative is 15 minutes of preparation and 45 of reading; it preserves more reading but provides less preparation. Ask whether a trial shows gains large enough to justify the lost reading opportunity.
activity.whyAdequate: It makes the limited resource explicit and compares benefits, costs, and affected students without inventing guaranteed gains.

exitTicket.title: Sharing the community room
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: A community center has six evening room-hours to allocate each week. It currently offers six hours of homework help. A proposal would use two hours for art and four for homework help. Some students have no quiet study space at home. No results for the art program are available.
exitTicket.output: Write a benefit, cost, and affected group; recommend a six-hour allocation with a reason; ask one useful question.
steps: Identify a possible gain from art and the loss from reducing homework help, including who may be affected.
Choose hours for art and homework help totaling six, and explain your priority and its cost.
Name one question about outcomes or needs that could change your recommendation.
exitTicket.check: Does your allocation total six, and have you acknowledged the cost of your preferred option?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Art offers an additional creative activity; reducing homework help removes two supported study hours, affecting students without quiet space. One defensible plan is one hour of art and five of homework help, prioritizing study access while allowing some art; it offers less art time than the proposal. Ask how many students depend on each homework-help hour and what benefits an art trial shows. Other feasible allocations can be justified with different priorities.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The answer makes the limited resource, affected students, and priority explicit without claiming a uniquely correct allocation or invented program results.

discussion.prompt: Can two reasonable recommendations use the same facts?
discussion.guidance: Yes. People may give different weight to study access, creativity, or other aims. Each should state its priority, acknowledge costs, and use the facts accurately.

discussion.prompt: What is known about the test-preparation benefit?
discussion.guidance: More practice time is expected, but improved scores have not been demonstrated. Keep the immediate allocation separate from the hoped-for result.

misconceptions.misconception: A benefit makes a proposal best overall.
misconceptions.response: Compare the gain with costs, lost opportunities, and who is affected.

misconceptions.misconception: A prediction is already a demonstrated result.
misconceptions.response: Label expected benefits as possibilities until suitable evidence supports them.

misconceptions.misconception: There must be one correct allocation.
misconceptions.response: Different priorities may support different feasible plans. Evaluate the reasoning and evidence, not agreement with one preference.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Draw a 60-minute bar for the main task. Label preparation and reading, then use the headings gain, loss, affected group. Expected example: 15 minutes for preparation and 45 for reading preserves more reading but supplies less preparation than the proposal.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask whether dividing time equally is automatically fairest. Expected response: no; equal time is one rule, but needs, benefits, and access may justify another allocation. Any proposed rule should state its purpose and costs.

assessmentCriteria: Benefits, costs, and an affected group are identified without inventing outcomes.
The proposed allocation fits the stated resource limit and explains its priority and cost.
The follow-up question could inform the decision while allowing different reasonable priorities.

packs.title: Change your mind in proportion
packs.subtitle: Revise confidence according to the relevance and strength of new evidence.
packs.format: Individual writing, pairs, and class discussion
objectives: State whether new evidence should raise, lower, or barely change confidence.
Explain why stronger relevant evidence deserves a larger update.
Keep a conclusion qualified when important details are missing.
materials: One student handout per learner, or display the activities and use paper.
Pens or pencils; no student devices required.
Instructor guide with model answers, kept separate from the handout.
preparation: Read the three scenarios and their model answers.
Print the three-page handout or display one activity at a time.
Explain that all scenarios and figures are invented for reasoning practice.

vocabulary.definition: How strongly you believe a claim is true.
Information that bears on the particular claim being evaluated.
Using chance to decide which group receives a change, helping make groups comparable.

timeline.title: Match evidence to the claim
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the reading-app warm-up. Distinguish liking an app from learning more.

timeline.title: Compare two lighting reports
timeline.instructions: Pairs complete the lighting activity. Require a reason for both the direction and relative size of each update, without exact confidence percentages.

timeline.title: Discuss strength and limits
timeline.instructions: Use the model answer and prompts. Explain that stronger evidence can justify greater confidence while leaving questions about size and reliability.

timeline.title: Revise a different belief
timeline.instructions: Learners complete the reminder exit ticket independently. Assess evidence relevance, proportionate revision, and a useful missing detail.

warmup.title: Does liking an app prove learning?
warmup.scenario: Invented scenario: You are unsure whether a reading app improves comprehension. A friend says its colors are attractive. A report then describes a fair comparison in which app users answer more comprehension questions correctly than a similar group using usual materials; no details about the size of the difference are supplied.
warmup.output: Write how each report should affect confidence and one remaining question.
steps: Explain whether the comment about colors bears on comprehension.
Say whether the comparison should raise or lower confidence, relative to starting unsure.
Name one missing detail needed before making a strong claim.
warmup.check: Have you changed confidence for the learning result while keeping its limits visible?
warmup.modelAnswer: The color comment should change confidence about comprehension very little. The stated fair comparison should raise confidence more because it measures comprehension directly. I would ask how large the difference was and how reliably it was measured before making a strong claim.
warmup.whyAdequate: The answer gives more weight to relevant outcome evidence without inventing a precise effect or confidence number.

activity.title: What should two studies change?
activity.scenario: Invented scenario: You begin unsure whether brighter streetlights reduce theft reports. Study A is one resident saying a street feels safer. Study B assigns 40 similar streets at random to brighter or unchanged lighting, keeps patrol policy the same, and records the same theft measure before and after: reports fall more in the brighter-light group. No exact effect size or uncertainty estimate is supplied.
activity.output: Write one update for each study, a comparison of their strength, and one missing detail you would seek.
steps: For each study, say whether it should raise, lower, or leave your confidence roughly unchanged, and explain why.
Choose which should change confidence more, using the difference between personal impressions and a controlled comparison.
Name one missing detail you would seek before making a strong conclusion. Do not invent a precise percentage change in confidence.
activity.check: Have you updated more for the stronger relevant evidence while keeping uncertainty about the size and reliability of the effect?
activity.modelAnswer: Study A should change confidence about theft reports very little: feeling safer is a different outcome and one person's impression. Study B should raise confidence more because random assignment and consistent measurement provide a fairer comparison of the claimed outcome. I would request the size of the difference and its uncertainty before making a strong claim.
activity.whyAdequate: It ties the direction and strength of the update to evidence quality and acknowledges that the scenario cannot justify an exact confidence number.

exitTicket.title: Do reminders prevent missed deadlines?
exitTicket.scenario: Invented scenario: You tentatively believe reminder messages reduce missed deadlines. Report A says one user likes the messages. Report B randomly assigns 200 students to reminders or no reminders for the same four-week course, uses the same deadline rules, and reports nearly equal missed-deadline rates. Exact rates and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
exitTicket.output: Write how each report should change your confidence, which matters more, and one question still open.
steps: Judge how much the approval report bears on missed deadlines.
State the direction of the update from the comparison and explain why it matters more.
Name a missing detail and explain why the report does not prove reminders can never help.
exitTicket.check: Have you allowed contrary evidence to weaken the belief without turning one result into a universal verdict?
exitTicket.modelAnswer: Report A should change confidence very little: liking messages is not fewer missed deadlines. Report B should lower confidence in a meaningful benefit for this setting because it compares the claimed outcome under random assignment. I would ask for the exact difference and its uncertainty. Nearly equal reported rates do not prove no possible benefit in any course or group.
exitTicket.whyAdequate: The answer responds to contrary evidence, weights the controlled comparison more strongly, and limits the conclusion to what the incomplete report supports.

discussion.prompt: Does stronger evidence require complete certainty?
discussion.guidance: No. It can justify a larger change while leaving uncertainty about the size, reliability, or reach of the result.

discussion.prompt: Why avoid exact confidence percentages here?
discussion.guidance: The scenarios do not supply enough information to calculate them. Explain the direction and relative strength of the change instead of pretending to numerical precision.

misconceptions.misconception: Changing a belief means admitting all earlier reasoning was worthless.
misconceptions.response: A reasonable starting view can change when relevant evidence improves. Revision can be a sign of careful thinking.

misconceptions.misconception: One strong report settles every setting.
misconceptions.response: Check the outcome, groups, methods, and missing details before extending the conclusion.

misconceptions.misconception: Fairness requires keeping the same confidence.
misconceptions.response: Relevant evidence should matter. Avoid both ignoring it and overreacting beyond what it shows.

adaptations.label: More support
adaptations.instructions: Offer three direction labels: raise, lower, very little change. Require one reason naming the measured outcome before comparing the size of the updates. Expected example: the color comment changes confidence very little; the fair comprehension comparison raises it, with questions about effect size remaining.

adaptations.label: More challenge
adaptations.instructions: Ask: If five news stories repeat the same study, are they five independent confirmations? Expected response: no; they share one underlying result. Separate repetition from new evidence before increasing confidence further.

assessmentCriteria: The direction of each update matches the evidence and the starting belief.
The stronger update is justified by relevance and method rather than confidence of presentation.
The conclusion names a meaningful uncertainty and avoids invented precision or universal certainty.
